source: NCERT Class X, India and the Contemporary World II, History Ch. 5.

sections.heading: 1. The First Printed Books — East Asia
points: The earliest print technology was developed in **China, Japan and Korea** — a system of **hand printing** (rubbing paper against inked woodblocks).
**China** was the major producer of printed material; books were printed for the civil service examinations conducted by the imperial state.
The **oldest Japanese printed book** is the Buddhist **Diamond Sutra (868 AD)**; Buddhist missionaries spread hand-printing to Japan.

sections.heading: 2. Print Comes to Europe
points: **Marco Polo** brought knowledge of woodblock printing from China to Italy (1295).
**Johann Gutenberg** developed the first-known **printing press** in **Strasbourg (1430s–1448)**; the **Gutenberg Bible** was the first printed book (about 180 copies).
The **Print Revolution** transformed lives — books became cheaper and more plentiful; a **new reading public** emerged as reading spread beyond the elite.

sections.heading: 3. Print and Change — Reformation and Ideas
points: **Martin Luther's** writings (Ninety-Five Theses, 1517) spread rapidly through print, leading to the **Protestant Reformation**; Luther said 'Printing is the ultimate gift of God'.
The **Roman Church** imposed control — an **Index of Prohibited Books (1558)** — fearing heresy and dissent.
Print encouraged debate, dissent and the **Enlightenment**; thinkers like **Rousseau and Voltaire** were widely read; print helped create conditions for the **French Revolution**.

sections.heading: 4. Print Comes to India
points: The **printing press first came to Goa** with **Portuguese missionaries** in the mid-16th century.
**James Augustus Hickey** began the **Bengal Gazette (1780)**, a weekly magazine — the first English newspaper printed in India.

Print fuelled **religious and social reform** and debate: **Raja Rammohun Roy** published the **Sambad Kaumudi (1821)**; orthodox Hindus brought out the Samachar Chandrika; Muslim ulama used cheap **Persian and Urdu** tracts.

sections.heading: 5. Print, Reform, Women and Nationalism
points: Print reached **women, workers and the poor**; reformers debated **widow remarriage, child marriage** and women's education; women like **Rashsundari Debi, Kailashbashini Debi, Tarabai Shinde and Pandita Ramabai** wrote about women's lives.
Cheap **'battala' publications** in Bengal and public libraries spread reading among the poor.
Print helped nationalism: it spread ideas of freedom; the **Vernacular Press Act (1878)**, modelled on Irish law, imposed **censorship** on Indian-language newspapers after 1857.
Nationalist newspapers grew despite repression; when **Bal Gangadhar Tilak** was imprisoned (1908), it sparked protest.

sections.heading: 6. High-Yield One-Liners (Last-Minute Recall)
points: Print began in China/Japan/Korea (hand printing); oldest Japanese book = Diamond Sutra (868 AD).
Gutenberg = first printing press (1430s); Gutenberg Bible = first printed book.
Martin Luther + print → Protestant Reformation; Church's Index of Prohibited Books (1558).
Press came to India in Goa (Portuguese); Bengal Gazette (Hickey, 1780) = first English newspaper.
Raja Rammohun Roy → Sambad Kaumudi (1821); Vernacular Press Act (1878) = censorship of Indian-language press.

sections.heading: 7. Common Traps (Watch Out)
points: **Print technology originated in China**, NOT Europe; Gutenberg developed the press in Europe.
The **Diamond Sutra (868 AD)** is the oldest Japanese printed book.
The **Vernacular Press Act (1878)** targeted **Indian-language (vernacular)** newspapers, not English ones.
**Hickey's Bengal Gazette (1780)** was the first English newspaper in India.
